summary: McKinleyville stretches across 21 square miles of coastal terrace land perched above the Pacific just north of Humboldt Bay, yet it holds only about 17,000 residents — a density of roughly 813 people per square mile that gives it the spacious, unhurried feel of a rural community that happens to have grocery stores and stoplights. The Hammond Trail, a paved coastal path running along ocean bluffs through former railroad right-of-way, offers the kind of evening walk most towns would build an entire tourism campaign around, and Clam Beach sits minutes away for open-sand access. The economy leans heavily on Humboldt State University (now Cal Poly Humboldt) and healthcare institutions clustered in nearby Arcata and Eureka — McKinleyville itself functions largely as a residential base, meaning most workers commute a short distance south along U.S. Route 101. A median home value of $414,200 against a median household income of $66,096 produces a price-to-income ratio above 6:1, which is steep but notably less brutal than coastal California's metros further south; median rent at $1,441 consumes roughly 26% of that median income pre-tax. Daily highs average just 60°F year-round under persistent marine influence — summers are cool and foggy more often than sunny, and winter lows rarely dip below the mid-40s. McKinleyville is essentially a place where the geography is extraordinary and the climate is relentlessly mild, but the tradeoff is geographic isolation and an economy with a narrow employer base.
